description: We are a passionate team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Taroudant, Morocco. We love technology, space exploration, coding, and innovation. Our goal is to build an interactive Martian map to explore terrain, identify hazards, and plan safe routes. We welcome teammates skilled in Python, web development, AI, data science, GIS, 3D design, or UI/UX. Creativity, curiosity, and teamwork are always welcome!
summary:
What we developed: ARES, an interactive web platform to explore Mars, analyze terrain hazards, plan energy-efficient routes and simulate a mission.

How it addresses the challenge: The challenge, Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, is about understanding the Martian surface to survive and move there. ARES turns NASA elevation and imagery data into a terrain map, flags hazards (slope, roughness, local relief, aspect), finds a path with an A* planner under a slope limit, and estimates oxygen use, EVA duration and return feasibility.

Why it is important: Mars terrain is rough and steep, and oxygen and time are limited, but the data is spread across many tools. ARES brings it into one workflow so a route can be tested before it is walked, and it makes space science hands-on for students. ARES is an educational prototype, not a certified safety tool.
details:
What exactly does it do? ARES lets users explore Mars from a global 3D globe down to Jezero Crater, analyze terrain hazards, plan a route between two points, and simulate the walk before it happens.

How does it work? NASA elevation and imagery data are converted into an elevation grid (DEM). For each cell, ARES computes slope, roughness, local relief and aspect to locate hazardous areas. An A* path planner searches the grid using an energy cost model and a user-selected slope limit. A simulator then estimates the oxygen budget, EVA duration and return feasibility under configured assumptions. Every dataset and place is labelled by reliability (available / pending check / planned; verified / approximate / fictional).

What benefits does it have? One tool replaces several separate ones. Users see why the shortest path is not always the cheapest in energy. Students and teachers can learn slope, energy and pathfinding through a real planet.

What do you hope to achieve? To make Mars data usable for decisions, support safer and better-informed thinking about future exploration, and make space science accessible and hands-on.

Limits: ARES gives estimates, not certified mission-safety results. Soil type, dust, weather and communications are not yet modelled; detailed coverage is limited to Jezero Crater.

Tools, languages, software:ARES is a web application built with React and TypeScript, bundled with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS. The 2D map uses Leaflet and the 3D globe uses CesiumJS. Elevation rasters are read with GeoTIFF.js and processed with Turf.js. Terrain analysis (slope, roughness, local relief, aspect) is computed from a DEM in TypeScript, and routes are found with an A* pathfinding algorithm. Tests use Vitest and Playwright. The project is hosted on GitHub and deployed on Vercel.

Source code: https://github.com/amine-CS96/ARES-Mars-Explorer

Use of AI: The team defined the idea, the workflow and the technical approach. AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) was used for [coding, debugging and troubleshooting; writing, editing and translation; the presentation; visual design]. Code written with AI assistance is marked in the repository README. No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified.
